reigns.tagline: The king who wouldn't cut his hair until Norway was his
reigns.reignEnded: Handed power to his son Eric
reigns.previously: Norway is a patchwork of petty kings, and Viking ships roam Europe.
paragraphs: Around 870, Norway was a long coast of rival chiefs and petty kings. Young men went raiding in England, Ireland and France and came home rich. Harald was the son of one of those small kings, Halfdan the Black. According to the sagas he took over as a boy of ten and spent the next years beating, buying off or driving out every rival he could reach.

His big moment came in a sea battle at Hafrsfjord, near today's Stavanger. Tradition dates it to 872; many historians now put it in the 880s. Harald won, and the western coast was his. Some beaten chiefs went off to settle Iceland, Orkney and Shetland. He had a lot of wives and a lot of sons, maybe as many as twenty. That was a problem waiting to happen, and in his old age he named one favourite son, Eric, as top king over the rest.

claims.text: Harald swore not to cut or comb his hair until he ruled all Norway, after a girl named Gyda refused to marry a petty king.
claims.note: Snorri tells it around 1230, three centuries later. It neatly explains the nickname, which is exactly why historians are wary of it.

claims.text: Hafrsfjord made Harald king of all Norway.
claims.note: Historians think he held mainly the west coast. Inland areas and Trøndelag stayed under local jarls and chiefs.

claims.text: Settlers fled to Iceland to escape Harald's tyranny.
claims.note: The Icelandic sagas love this story because it made their ancestors freedom-lovers. Land hunger probably mattered just as much.

reigns.hook: Old Harald has crowned Eric king over all his brothers. The brothers have ships and followers of their own, and none of them plans to bow quietly.

reigns.tagline: The brother-killer who ended up king of York
reigns.cameToPower: Named top king by his father
reigns.reignEnded: Pushed out when Haakon came home
reigns.previously: Old Harald Fairhair hands his kingdom to his favourite son, Eric.
paragraphs: Eric had his father's blessing and almost nobody else's. The sagas say he went after his own half-brothers one by one, and a twelfth-century Latin writer calls him a killer of brothers. His wife Gunnhild became the great villain of saga literature: clever, ruthless and said to know magic. Norwegians soon had enough of the pair of them.

When his young half-brother Haakon arrived from England, the farmers flocked to him and Eric had to leave. He didn't vanish. A king named Eric ruled the Vikings of York, on and off, until 954, and coins with his name on them survive. He was driven out of York that year and killed in an ambush, probably at Stainmore in the Pennines. Gunnhild and their sons went to Denmark and waited.

claims.text: Eric killed several of his half-brothers to secure the throne.
claims.note: The sagas and twelfth-century histories all say so, but they were written 250 years later. Nothing from Eric's own time survives on it.

claims.text: Eric Bloodaxe and Eric, king of York, were the same man.
claims.note: Later sagas and English chroniclers say yes. Historian Clare Downham argued in 2004 that the York king may have been a different Eric.

claims.text: Gunnhild learned witchcraft from two Sami sorcerers.
claims.note: A story in Heimskringla. It belongs to the sagas' habit of painting Gunnhild as a witch-queen.

reigns.hook: Eric is gone and Norway has a new king, his youngest half-brother. Haakon grew up at the English court as a Christian, and he has a promise the farmers love.

reigns.tagline: The English-raised Christian who ruled a pagan land
reigns.reignEnded: Killed at the Battle of Fitjar
reigns.previously: Eric Bloodaxe has worn out his welcome. Norway wants a new king.
paragraphs: Haakon was Harald Fairhair's youngest son, sent as a boy to be fostered by King Æthelstan of England. He grew up baptised, well-read and polished. When he sailed home as a teenager he made the farmers an offer: he would give back the family land rights his father had taken. That won the Trøndelag assembly in a day, and Eric was finished.

Haakon was good at the job. The sagas credit him with organising the coast into districts that had to supply warships and crews, and with lighting chains of warning beacons on the hills. He tried to bring in Christianity and got nowhere. The pagan chiefs pushed back hard, and he backed down. Eric's sons kept raiding with Danish help, and around 961 they caught him at Fitjar. Haakon won the battle but took an arrow and died.

claims.text: The chiefs forced Haakon to eat horsemeat at a pagan sacrificial feast.
claims.note: Snorri tells it in detail, but he wrote nearly 300 years later. It works as a tidy symbol of the king losing the religious argument.

claims.text: A poem welcomed Haakon into Valhalla, Christian or not.
claims.note: Hákonarmál by the skald Eyvind the Plagiarist survives. It shows the gods receiving Haakon after Fitjar.

claims.text: Haakon set up the coastal warship levy and the beacon chain.
claims.note: The sagas say so. Historians suspect later systems were credited back to a famous king.

reigns.hook: Haakon dies with no son to follow him. Eric's sons have Danish backing and their mother Gunnhild steering them, and the eldest, Harald, is ready to take the throne.

reigns.tagline: Gunnhild's son, lured to his death in Denmark
reigns.cameToPower: Took the throne with his brothers
reigns.reignEnded: Killed in an ambush at Hals
reigns.previously: Haakon the Good wins at Fitjar but dies of an arrow wound.
paragraphs: Harald was the eldest surviving son of Eric Bloodaxe and Gunnhild. He took Norway with his brothers and with the backing of the Danish king Harald Bluetooth. Gunnhild was the real power behind them, at least in the sagas. The brothers were Christians and broke up pagan shrines, and they spent years fighting the chiefs who wouldn't bow.

The biggest of those chiefs was Sigurd, Jarl of Lade, near Trondheim. Gunnhild's sons trapped him and burned him in a house. His son Haakon fled to Denmark and plotted revenge with Bluetooth. Around 970 Greycloak was invited to Denmark and sailed into the Limfjord. At Hals he was cut down by a Danish prince called Gold-Harald, and Bluetooth took Norway for himself.

claims.text: Harald got his nickname by buying a grey sheepskin cloak no one else wanted.
claims.note: Snorri says an Icelandic trader couldn't sell his cloaks until the king took one, and then the whole court copied him. A good story with no early witness.

claims.text: Norway suffered terrible hunger under Gunnhild's sons.
claims.note: The sagas say so, and a skaldic verse speaks of snow in midsummer. Saga writers liked to blame bad harvests on unpopular kings.

claims.text: Haakon Jarl and Harald Bluetooth planned the ambush together.
claims.note: Heimskringla tells the full plot. Earlier sources only agree that Harald died in Denmark.

reigns.hook: Greycloak lies dead on a Danish shore. The man who set the trap, Haakon of Lade, comes home to rule Norway, and he means to bring back the old gods.

reigns.title: Haakon Jarl
reigns.tagline: Norway's last great pagan lord
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Son of Sigurd, Jarl of Lade
reigns.previously: Harald Greycloak is lured to Denmark and cut down at Hals.
paragraphs: Haakon never called himself king. He was Jarl of Lade, ruling Norway for the Danish king Harald Bluetooth, and that suited him fine. He reopened the pagan temples and brought back the sacrifices. When the harvests got better, people took it as the gods' approval. His court poets praised him as the man who had restored the old faith.

He soon slipped Danish control and stopped paying tribute. Around 986 a fleet of Danish raiders, the Jomsvikings, attacked him at Hjørungavåg, and Haakon smashed them. In his later years the sagas say he grew greedy and took other men's wives. In 995 the Trønders rose against him just as a new rival landed. Haakon hid on a farm with a single slave, Kark, who killed him.

claims.text: Haakon hid in a pigsty and was killed by his slave Kark, who then took his head to Olaf Tryggvason.
claims.note: Snorri's version. Olaf is said to have rewarded Kark by beheading him too. Nobody doubts Haakon died in 995; the pigsty is saga colour.

claims.text: At Hjørungavåg, Haakon sacrificed his own son to bring down a hailstorm on the Jomsvikings.
claims.note: Found in Jómsvíkinga saga and Snorri, written over 200 years later.

claims.text: Haakon beat the Jomsvikings at Hjørungavåg.
claims.note: His court poets celebrated the victory. Historians accept the battle, though its date is uncertain.

reigns.hook: Haakon is dead and Trøndelag hails a new king. Olaf Tryggvason is a great-grandson of Harald Fairhair, rich from raiding England and a baptised Christian in a hurry.

reigns.tagline: The Viking who converted Norway at sword-point
reigns.cameToPower: Hailed king as Haakon Jarl fell
reigns.previously: Haakon Jarl dies on a farm, killed by his own slave.
paragraphs: Olaf grew up in exile and made his name as a Viking. In 994 he and the Danish prince Svein Forkbeard attacked London. King Æthelred of England paid them off, and Olaf was confirmed as a Christian with Æthelred as his sponsor. He promised never to raid England again, and he kept his word. The next year he sailed to Norway and took the throne.

He spread Christianity the hard way. Chiefs who refused baptism were threatened, maimed or killed, and he leaned hard on Iceland too, which accepted the faith around 1000. He built a great warship, the Long Serpent. In September 1000 his enemies caught him at Svolder in the Baltic: the Danish and Swedish kings, plus Haakon Jarl's son Eric. When his ship was taken, Olaf jumped into the sea in his armour.

claims.text: As a boy, Olaf was sold as a slave in Estonia and later raised at the court of Kyiv.
claims.note: Told by the Icelandic monk Oddr Snorrason and by Snorri, both writing about 200 years later.

claims.text: Olaf was confirmed at Andover, with King Æthelred as his sponsor.
claims.note: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records it under 994 and calls him Anlaf.

claims.text: Olaf survived Svolder and lived on as a monk in the East.
claims.note: Rumours of his survival appear in the sagas almost at once. No evidence backs them.

reigns.hook: With Olaf gone, Norway is carved up between the Danish and Swedish kings, with Haakon's sons as jarls. Far away, another Fairhair descendant, Olaf Haraldsson, is learning to fight.

reigns.tagline: Norway carved up after Svolder
reigns.previously: Olaf Tryggvason leaps into the sea at Svolder.
paragraphs: After Olaf Tryggvason died at the sea battle of Svolder in 1000, the winners divided Norway. The Danish king Sweyn Forkbeard and the Swedish king Olof took parts of the south and east, and the brothers Eric and Sweyn, jarls of Lade, ruled the rest for them.
Eric left in 1015 to help Cnut conquer England. That same year Olaf Haraldsson landed in Norway, and in 1016 he beat Jarl Sweyn at Nesjar.
reigns.hook: Olaf Haraldsson, the future saint, makes himself king of all Norway.

reigns.tagline: The Viking who became Norway's eternal king
reigns.cameToPower: Sailed home and beat Jarl Svein
reigns.reignEnded: Fled as the chiefs backed Cnut
reigns.previously: Olaf Tryggvason drowns at Svolder; jarls rule for foreign kings.
paragraphs: Olaf Haraldsson started raiding at about twelve and fought all over the Baltic, England and France. In 1015 he came home, and the next year he beat Jarl Svein at Nesjar to become king. He finished what Olaf Tryggvason had started. With his bishop Grimkell he set down church law for the whole country, and pagan practice was hunted down district by district.

He was tough and often brutal, and many chiefs hated him. Cnut, king of England and Denmark, bought their loyalty. In 1028 Cnut sailed in and Olaf fled to Kyiv. In 1030 he came back with a small army and met the farmers' host at Stiklestad on 29 July. He was killed. Within a year his body was dug up, reported uncorrupted, and declared holy. Norway's patron saint was born.

claims.text: The sun went dark during the Battle of Stiklestad.
claims.note: Snorri says so. There was an eclipse in 1030, but on 31 August, a month after the battle.

claims.text: When Olaf's coffin was opened, his hair and nails had kept growing.
claims.note: A classic saint's miracle, told by the sagas and the twelfth-century Passio Olavi.

claims.text: Cnut bribed Norwegian chiefs to desert Olaf.
claims.note: Olaf's own poet Sigvat says it in a surviving verse, and the sagas agree.

reigns.hook: Olaf has run to Russia. Cnut now rules England, Denmark and Norway, and the chiefs who betrayed Olaf are waiting to be paid.

reigns.tagline: The Danish emperor of the North Sea
reigns.cameToPower: Sailed in; the chiefs hailed him
reigns.reignEnded: Died in England; Norway in revolt
reigns.previously: Olaf II flees to Russia as the chiefs side with Cnut.
paragraphs: Cnut was the son of Svein Forkbeard. He had won England in 1016 and Denmark a couple of years later. In 1028 he sailed to Norway with a big fleet and was hailed as king, without a battle. He left Haakon, grandson of old Haakon Jarl, to run things. Haakon drowned within a year, and Olaf tried to win his crown back and died at Stiklestad.

So Cnut sent his young son Svein to rule Norway, with the boy's mother, Ælfgifu of Northampton. It went badly. They brought in new taxes and harsh Danish-style laws, and Norwegians started praying at Olaf's tomb instead. By 1035 the same chiefs who had betrayed Olaf wanted his son. Svein fled to Denmark, and on 12 November Cnut died at Shaftesbury in England.

claims.text: Cnut sat on the shore and ordered the tide to turn back.
claims.note: First told by Henry of Huntingdon about a century later, as a lesson in humility, not foolishness.

claims.text: Norwegians remembered the rule of Ælfgifu and Svein as a hard time.
claims.note: The skald Sigvat calls it 'Ælfgifu's time', and the sagas list the new dues.

claims.text: Cnut called himself king of all England, Denmark, Norway and part of the Swedes.
claims.note: He uses the title in his letter to the English of 1027.

reigns.hook: Two chiefs who fought against St Olaf, Einar and Kalv, are heading east to Russia. They want to bring back his eleven-year-old son.

start.note: Proclaimed in 1035 as Cnut's regent fled; sole king from Cnut's death

reigns.cameToPower: Fetched from Russia by the chiefs
reigns.previously: Cnut dies in England, and his son Svein has fled Norway.
paragraphs: Magnus was Olaf's son by a servant woman, born in 1024 and raised in exile at Kyiv. In 1035 the chiefs who had turned on his father brought him home, and the eleven-year-old was hailed king. At first he went after the men who had fought at Stiklestad. Then Sigvat, his father's old poet, warned him in blunt verses to stop. Magnus listened, and that's how he became 'the Good'.

He made a pact with Cnut's son Harthacnut: whoever died first, the other would take his kingdom. Harthacnut died in 1042 and Magnus became king of Denmark. In 1043 he crushed a Wendish army at Lyrskog Heath. In 1046 he agreed to share Norway with his uncle, Harald Hardrada, back from Constantinople. In October 1047 Magnus died in Denmark, aged 23, with no son.

claims.text: Magnus was named after Charlemagne, Carolus Magnus.
claims.note: Snorri says Sigvat chose the name at the baby's baptism. Plausible, but only the sagas tell it.

claims.text: Sigvat's 'Plain-speaking Verses' turned Magnus from revenge.
claims.note: The poem, Bersöglisvísur, survives and lectures the young king directly.

claims.text: Magnus died after falling from his horse.
claims.note: Some sagas blame a fall, others a sudden illness. All agree it was quick.

reigns.hook: Magnus is dead with no heir. Denmark goes to Svein Estridsen, but Norway now belongs to his uncle Harald: veteran of Constantinople, loaded with gold, and no gentleman.

reigns.tagline: The Viking mercenary who wanted England too
reigns.cameToPower: Co-king, then alone when Magnus died
reigns.reignEnded: Arrow in the throat, Stamford Bridge
reigns.previously: Magnus the Good is dead, and his uncle Harald now rules alone.
paragraphs: Harald was St Olaf's half-brother. At 15 he fought beside Olaf at Stiklestad, got wounded, and slipped away to Russia. From there he went south to Constantinople and joined the Varangian Guard, the Byzantine emperor's Viking bodyguard. He fought in Sicily and Bulgaria, and came home years later loaded with gold and married to a Russian princess, Elisiv, daughter of Yaroslav the Wise.

Back in Norway in 1046 he got his nephew Magnus to share the throne, paying for it with a slice of his treasure. A year later Magnus was dead and Harald ruled alone. He spent the next 17 years attacking Denmark, trying to wrench it from Sweyn Estridsen. He won fights, including a big sea battle at Niså in 1062, but never the Danish crown. In 1064 the two kings finally made peace.

In 1066 Harald sailed for England with about 300 ships, joined by Tostig, the English king's angry exiled brother. He smashed an English army at Fulford, outside York, on 20 September. Five days later King Harold Godwinson caught him off guard at Stamford Bridge. Harald took an arrow in the throat, and his army was cut to pieces. The Viking Age is often said to end right there.

claims.text: Harold Godwinson offered him “seven feet of English ground”, or a bit more, since he was so tall.
claims.note: The line comes from Snorri, writing about 160 years later. No English source records it.

claims.text: A Byzantine writer confirms that Harald served the emperor.
claims.note: Kekaumenos, an 11th-century Byzantine officer, mentions “Araltes”, a Norse king's son who fought in Sicily and Bulgaria and won imperial rank.

claims.text: Harald was thrown into prison in Constantinople and escaped with a noblewoman's help.
claims.note: The sagas tell it with relish. No Greek source mentions an arrest or an escape.

reigns.hook: Harald's son Olaf was guarding the ships and survived. The English king let him sail home with just 24 ships, after he swore never to come back. Norway needs a rest.

reigns.previously: Harald Hardrada dies at Stamford Bridge.
paragraphs: When Harald Hardrada sailed to invade England in 1066, he left his son Magnus behind as king. After Harald was killed at Stamford Bridge, Magnus shared Norway with his brother Olaf, who came home with the survivors.
Magnus ruled the north and west. He died of ringworm or a similar illness in 1069, aged about 21, and Olaf ruled alone.

reigns.tagline: The quiet king who gave Norway 26 years of peace
reigns.cameToPower: Shared the crown with brother Magnus
reigns.previously: Harald Hardrada falls at Stamford Bridge. His son Olaf sails home.
paragraphs: Olaf had sailed to England with his father but stayed with the ships, so he missed the slaughter at Stamford Bridge. Back in Norway he shared the crown with his brother Magnus II, who had been left at home. When Magnus died in 1069, Olaf ruled alone for more than 20 years, and for once nobody invaded anybody.

That calm was the whole point. Olaf made peace with Denmark and married Ingerid, daughter of the Danish king Sweyn. He gave the Church firm roots, with bishops settled in fixed seats, and built a stone Christ Church in Nidaros (Trondheim) over the grave of his uncle, St Olaf. Tradition says he founded Bergen, which grew into Norway's great trading town.

His nickname, Kyrre, means “the quiet” or “the peaceful”. He died of illness in 1093 at Haukbø in Ranrike, now part of western Sweden. His son Magnus was nothing like him: a restless fighter who couldn't sit still.

claims.text: King Harold of England let Olaf go home with 24 ships after he swore oaths of friendship.
claims.note: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle reports the oaths and the 24 ships.

claims.text: Olaf founded Bergen in about 1070.
claims.note: The date comes from Snorri. Archaeologists have found traces of settlement there that may be older.

claims.text: Peace made Norwegians showy, with costly new fashions and gold rings.
claims.note: Snorri describes it about 150 years later, and there is little else to check it against.

reigns.hook: Olaf's son Magnus is about 20, spoiling for a fight and said to dress like a Scot. He'll spend his reign at sea, and the Irish Sea is calling.

reigns.tagline: The bare-legged raider who wanted the Irish Sea
reigns.cameToPower: Hailed king; shared with cousin Haakon
reigns.previously: Peaceful Olaf Kyrre dies. His son Magnus is itching for a fight.
paragraphs: Magnus was about 20 when his father died, and at first he had to share Norway with his cousin Haakon. Haakon died in 1095, and Magnus crushed the chiefs who had backed him. Then he looked west. In 1098 he sailed to Orkney, packed its two earls off to Norway, and swept on through the Hebrides and the Isle of Man.

Off Anglesey he clashed with two Norman lords, both called Hugh, and one of them, Hugh of Montgomery, was killed by an arrow. King Edgar of Scots agreed that the western isles belonged to Norway. Back home Magnus fought Sweden over the border lands, until the kings of Norway, Sweden and Denmark met in 1101 and made peace.

In 1102 he went west again, this time to Ireland, and teamed up with the high king Muirchertach Ua Briain. His son Sigurd married the Irish king's daughter. In August 1103, while waiting for cattle and supplies in Ulster, Magnus and his men were ambushed. He was killed, aged about 30, and his three young sons inherited Norway.

claims.text: He got his nickname by going bare-legged in the short tunics of the western isles.
claims.note: Snorri says so, writing over a century later. Other explanations were also told, and none can be checked.

claims.text: To claim Kintyre as an island, he had his ship dragged across its neck of land with himself at the helm.
claims.note: The story is in Snorri and the Orkney sagas, written about a century later. Scottish sources don't mention it.

claims.text: When warned about his reckless raids, he said kings are made for glory, not long life.
claims.note: The line is reported in the sagas long after his death. It sounds like him, which is the trouble.

reigns.hook: Three boys now share the crown. One of them, Sigurd, will soon sail further than any Norwegian king before him: all the way to Jerusalem.

reigns.tagline: The first king from the north to reach Jerusalem
reigns.cameToPower: Shared the crown with two brothers
reigns.previously: Magnus Barefoot is killed in Ulster. Three boys share his crown.
paragraphs: Sigurd shared Norway with his brothers Eystein and Olaf. In 1107 he left them to mind the kingdom and set off on crusade with about 60 ships. He spent the winter in England, fought Muslim garrisons in Portugal, and cleared out pirates on the Balearic Islands as he worked his way across the Mediterranean.

In 1110 he reached the Holy Land. King Baldwin of Jerusalem rode with him to the River Jordan, and Sigurd's fleet helped Baldwin capture the port of Sidon. His reward was a splinter said to come from the True Cross. He sailed on to Constantinople, gave his ships to the emperor, and went home overland.

Back in Norway he was a star. Olaf died in 1115 and Eystein in 1123, leaving Sigurd sole king. The sagas say his last years were darkened by fits of rage. Then an Irishman named Harald Gille turned up claiming to be Magnus Barefoot's son. Sigurd accepted him as a brother, on condition he made no claim to the throne while Sigurd lived. Sigurd died in 1130.

claims.text: He rode into Constantinople on a horse shod with gold, and left a lost golden shoe lying in the street.
claims.note: A saga flourish from Snorri. Byzantine writers say nothing about it.

claims.text: Sigurd's fleet helped King Baldwin take Sidon in 1110.
claims.note: Fulcher of Chartres, a chronicler living in Jerusalem at the time, records the Norse fleet's part in the siege.

claims.text: Harald Gille proved he was Magnus Barefoot's son by walking over red-hot ploughshares.
claims.note: The sagas say he passed the ordeal. Whether he really was Magnus's son can't be checked.

reigns.hook: Sigurd's son Magnus and the Irish newcomer Harald Gille now split Norway between them. It won't last. One of them will end up blinded, crippled and shut away in a monastery.

reigns.title: Magnus the Blind and Harald Gille
reigns.tagline: Two kings, one kingdom, and a very nasty ending
reigns.cameToPower: Split the realm at Sigurd's death
reigns.previously: Sigurd the Crusader dies after 27 years. Who gets the crown now?
paragraphs: Sigurd the Crusader wanted his son Magnus to rule alone. The snag was Harald Gille, a newcomer raised in Ireland who had turned up around 1127 claiming Magnus Barefoot as his father. Sigurd had accepted him as a brother on one condition: no grab for the crown. The moment Sigurd died in 1130, Harald had himself hailed king at the Haugating in Tønsberg, and young Magnus had to split Norway with him.

For four years the two kings kept an uneasy peace. Magnus, proud and short-tempered, wanted his uncle gone. On 9 August 1134 he smashed Harald's army at Fyrileiv in Bohuslän, and Harald ran to Denmark. Magnus thought the war was won. He sent his men home and went to spend the winter in Bergen.

Big mistake. Harald came back with Danish help and reached Bergen before Christmas. On 7 January 1135 he took the town. The harbour had been chained shut, so Magnus could not sail away. Harald's men put out his eyes, cut off a foot and castrated him, then shut him in the monastery on Munkholmen, off Nidaros. A maimed man, everyone assumed, could never be king again.

claims.text: Harald Gille really was Magnus Barefoot's son.
claims.note: His only proof was passing an ordeal by fire. Magnus Barefoot had spent time in Ireland, so it's possible, but it can't be checked.

claims.text: Magnus was blinded, castrated and lost a foot on Harald's orders.
claims.note: All the main sagas tell it, and his nickname stuck. The details come from writers about a century later.

claims.text: Bergen's harbour was closed with a chain so Magnus could not escape by sea.
claims.note: Snorri quotes a verse by the court poet Einar Skúlason, who lived through these years, about the harbour being shut.

reigns.hook: Harald Gille is sole king now. But he isn't the only man in Norway claiming Magnus Barefoot as his father, and the other one is a former deacon with a grudge.

reigns.tagline: The Irish-raised king who blinded his nephew
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Uncle of the king he blinded
reigns.previously: Harald Gille takes Bergen and has his nephew Magnus blinded.
paragraphs: Harald Gille was an unusual Norwegian king. He grew up in Ireland, and the sagas paint him as easy-going and open-handed, happy to give his friends whatever they asked. He could also be ruthless. He had Reinald, Bishop of Stavanger, hanged for refusing to hand over Magnus's treasure. From 1135 he ruled the whole country alone, and he married well: his queen, Ingrid, was a granddaughter of a Swedish king.

Then Sigurd Slembe arrived. He was a former deacon who said that he, too, was a son of Magnus Barefoot, and he wanted his share. Harald refused. On the night of 14 December 1136, after a feast, Sigurd and his men broke into the house in Bergen where Harald lay asleep and killed him in his bed.

Sigurd expected the country to come over to him. It didn't. Harald's men refused to serve a king-killer, outlawed him, and hailed Harald's little sons as kings instead. Harald left four boys by different mothers, and every one of them would wear the crown.

claims.text: Sigurd Slembe was really Magnus Barefoot's son.
claims.note: Like Harald, he had only his own word and an ordeal to back him. Nobody can check it now.

claims.text: Harald's Norse was so poor at first that people laughed at him.
claims.note: Morkinskinna and Snorri tell how he was mocked for his speech. A nice touch, but written a century later.

claims.text: 'Gille' comes from the Irish Gilla Críst, 'servant of Christ'.
claims.note: His full Norse nickname, Gillikristr, supports it, and most name scholars accept it, but it is still an interpretation.

reigns.hook: Norway now has two toddler kings, three-year-old Sigurd and one-year-old Inge, and a killer on the loose. Sigurd Slembe still has one card to play: the blind man in the monastery.

reigns.title: Sigurd Munn and Inge
reigns.tagline: Baby brothers on the throne, until they grew up
reigns.previously: Harald Gille is murdered in his bed. His killer is refused the crown.
paragraphs: When Harald Gille died, his sons were tiny. Sigurd, about three, was hailed king at the Øyrating in Trøndelag. Inge, barely one, was hailed at the Borgarting near Sarpsborg. A third baby, Magnus, was made king too. Real power lay with their father's barons and with Inge's mother, Queen Ingrid, who ran the country in the boys' names.

The guardians first had to deal with Sigurd Slembe and blind Magnus, and they beat them in 1139. In 1142 a fourth brother, Eystein, arrived from Scotland and got his share. Little Magnus died in the 1140s. In 1152 or 1153 Norway got its own archbishop at Nidaros. For years the boys' guardians kept the peace.

When the old guardians died and the brothers came of age, suspicion took over. In 1155 the three kings were due to meet in Bergen. Inge accused the others of plotting to depose him, one of Sigurd's men killed one of Inge's, and Inge's men stormed the house where Sigurd was staying. Sigurd, aged about 22, was cut down. Eystein turned up too late to help.

claims.text: Sigurd and Eystein were plotting to strip Inge of his crown.
claims.note: That's the sagas' version, and the sagas favour Inge. Some historians think it was Inge's excuse for striking first.

claims.text: Inge became a hunchback after being carried into battle as a toddler in 1137.
claims.note: Snorri and Morkinskinna say so. The Danish writer Saxo says a maid dropped him as a baby. Nobody really knows.

claims.text: Sigurd's nickname Munn means 'mouth'.
claims.note: Snorri describes him as strong and well built but with an ugly mouth.

reigns.hook: Inge has won the fight in Bergen, but Eystein is still out there. First, though, rewind to 1137: Harald Gille's killer is on his way to fetch the blind king from his monastery.

reigns.title: Sigurd Slembe and Magnus the Blind
reigns.tagline: A king-killer and a blind king against the boy kings
reigns.cameToPower: Fetched blind Magnus from a monastery
reigns.previously: Sigurd Munn is dead. Rewind to 1136 and Harald Gille's killer.
paragraphs: Sigurd Slembe had killed a king and got nothing for it. He had trained as a deacon before he turned adventurer, and his nickname probably means something like 'the noisy one'. Outlawed by Harald's men, he needed a figurehead, and he found one on Munkholmen: Magnus the Blind, still a king's son even without his eyes. In 1137 Magnus left the monastery and joined him.

It went badly. Magnus was beaten at Minne by the boy king Inge's men and fled to Sweden and Denmark. A Danish invasion on his behalf came to nothing. Back together, the two claimants had little support at home and lived more like pirates than kings, raiding the coast with a small fleet.

On 12 November 1139 they met the boy kings' fleet at Holmengrå, near Hvaler in the Oslofjord. Magnus was killed on his ship. Sigurd jumped overboard but was caught, and Inge's men tortured him slowly to death. Harald Gille's sons were safe, and the first round of Norway's civil wars was over.

claims.text: Sigurd Slembe was tortured to death after Holmengrå.
claims.note: The sagas describe the torture in grim detail. Some of that may be dressed up, but his execution is not doubted.

claims.text: As Magnus fell, a loyal guard held him up and one spear went through them both.
claims.note: Snorri tells it. It is a heroic saga image with no other witness.

claims.text: Sigurd Slembe was a son of Magnus Barefoot.
claims.note: Nobody at the time could prove it either way, and his enemies called him a fraud.

reigns.hook: The rebels are dead and the boy kings are safe. Then, in 1142, a stranger sails in from Scotland. He says he is another son of Harald Gille, and he wants his share.

reigns.tagline: The Scottish-born king who went raiding like a Viking
reigns.reignEnded: Killed by Inge's men in Bohuslän
reigns.previously: Magnus the Blind and Sigurd Slembe die after Holmengrå.
paragraphs: Eystein was Harald Gille's son from his years in the west, born to a woman called Bjaðǫk and left behind when Harald sailed to Norway. Harald had let it be known that he had a boy over there. So in 1142 a group of Norwegian lords went to Scotland and brought Eystein and his mother home, and he was made king alongside his little half-brothers.

He had a taste for the old Viking life. In the early 1150s he took a fleet west, seized the Earl of Orkney in Caithness and made him pay a ransom, then raided down the Scottish coast to Aberdeen and on to England. At home he was thought clever but greedy, and that cost him friends.

After Sigurd Munn was killed in 1155, he and Inge patched things up, but not for long. In 1157 their armies met near Moster on the west coast, and Eystein's men simply melted away. He fled east, was caught in Bohuslän and was killed there on 21 August. Locals soon began to treat his grave as a holy place.

claims.text: Eystein sacked Whitby in England.
claims.note: The story comes from the sagas, written about 80 years later. No English chronicle confirms it.

claims.text: Inge ordered his brother's killing.
claims.note: People argued about it even at the time, and the sagas leave the question open.

claims.text: A spring welled up where Eystein was killed, and people came to it for healing.
claims.note: Snorri reports the local cult. His own party tried to make a saint of him, without success.

reigns.hook: Inge is the last brother standing. But Sigurd Munn left a little son, and Eystein's beaten men are about to make the boy their king.

reigns.tagline: The crippled king the barons loved
reigns.reignEnded: Killed on the ice at Oslo
reigns.previously: Eystein flees Inge's army and is killed in Bohuslän.
paragraphs: Inge could barely walk. He had a hump on his back and chest and one withered leg. Yet the sagas call him the best-looking of the brothers and the best liked. He let the great landowners help run the kingdom, and they backed him for it. His right-hand man was Gregorius Dagsson, a hard-bitten baron and his best commander.

With Sigurd and Eystein dead, Inge should have been safe. But their followers hailed Sigurd's ten-year-old son Haakon as king, and the war went on. Inge had the Church on his side and the bigger armies. Haakon's men had nothing left to lose.

In January 1161 Gregorius was killed in a fight on the ice with Haakon's men. A month later, on 3 February, Haakon's army came at Oslo. Part of Inge's army, led by Godred, the exiled King of the Isles, switched sides. Inge fought on the frozen fjord and was killed there, aged about 25. He was buried in St Hallvard's Church in Oslo.

claims.text: Godred of the Isles changed sides at the decisive moment.
claims.note: The sagas name him. He was a real exiled king of Man and the Isles who had joined Inge.

claims.text: Inge was killed fighting on the frozen fjord outside Oslo.
claims.note: All the sagas agree on a battle on the ice in February 1161.

claims.text: The barons loved Inge because he let them run things.
claims.note: That's Snorri's verdict. Modern historians tend to see the barons using a weak king for their own ends.

reigns.hook: Inge is dead and teenage Haakon holds the field. But Inge's party has found a new leader: Erling Skakke, a tough old crusader with a crooked neck and a five-year-old son with royal blood.

reigns.tagline: A boy king with a man's shoulders
reigns.previously: Inge dies fighting on the ice at Oslo. Haakon's men win the day.
paragraphs: Haakon was Sigurd Munn's son, born in 1147. When his uncle Eystein was killed in 1157, Eystein's and Sigurd's old followers needed a king's son to fight for, and ten-year-old Haakon was it. He was big for his age, with unusually broad shoulders, which gave him his nickname, Herdebrei.

For four years his men fought Inge up and down the country, and in February 1161 they finally killed him at Oslo. For a moment the teenager looked like the last king standing. But Inge's barons would not have him. They turned to Erling Skakke and declared Erling's little son Magnus king instead.

Erling was a far better general than anyone on Haakon's side. On 7 July 1162 he caught Haakon's fleet at Sekken, an island in the Romsdalsfjord. Haakon's men were routed and the boy king was killed, still only 15. His followers tried other sons of Sigurd Munn, but Erling hunted them down.

claims.text: Herdebrei means 'broad-shouldered'.
claims.note: The sagas explain the nickname by his size and build, even as a boy.

claims.text: After Sekken his followers hailed another son of Sigurd Munn, who was caught and put to death in 1163.
claims.note: Snorri names him Sigurd Markusfostre. Erling Skakke's men killed him in Bergen.

claims.text: Haakon was really Sigurd Munn's son.
claims.note: Unlike many claimants of the age, his parentage was not challenged by his enemies.

reigns.hook: With Haakon dead, Erling Skakke's boy Magnus has Norway to himself. But Magnus's royal blood comes only through his mother, so Erling needs something new: a crown, an archbishop and a coronation.

reigns.tagline: The first crowned king in Scandinavia
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Sigurd I's grandson, through his mother
reigns.cameToPower: Made king by his father, Erling
reigns.previously: Haakon Herdebrei is killed at Sekken. Erling's son is unrivalled.
paragraphs: Magnus had an awkward claim. His royal blood came through his mother, Kristin, Sigurd the Crusader's daughter, and no Norwegian king had ever taken the throne that way. His father, Erling Skakke, was a tough, clever nobleman who had been to the Holy Land. He found his answer in the Church.

In 1163 or 1164 Archbishop Eystein crowned the boy in Bergen, the first coronation in Scandinavia. A new law said the crown should pass to one legitimate son, with the bishops' approval. Erling ran the country, ruthlessly, for the next fifteen years, and hunted down every rival king's son he could find.

Then came Sverre, a priest from the Faroes who claimed to be Sigurd Munn's son and took over the ragged Birkebeiner rebels. In 1179 he killed Erling in battle at Kalvskinnet, outside Nidaros. Magnus fought on for five more years. On 15 June 1184 Sverre caught his fleet at Fimreite in the Sognefjord. Magnus's ship went down and he drowned, aged about 28.

claims.text: Magnus Erlingsson's coronation was the first in Scandinavia.
claims.note: Historians accept this. The exact year, 1163 or 1164, is still argued over.

claims.text: Magnus promised to rule Norway as a vassal of St Olaf.
claims.note: A privilege letter in his name says so, but historians argue over its date and how far it was ever meant seriously.

claims.text: Erling got his crooked neck, and his nickname Skakke, from a wound on crusade.
claims.note: The sagas tell of a sword cut to the neck in a sea fight in the Mediterranean. Nice story, hard to check.

reigns.hook: Magnus Erlingsson lies at the bottom of the fjord. The winner is a man nobody had heard of ten years earlier: a priest from the Faroe Islands who swears he is a king's son.

reigns.tagline: The priest who said he was a king's son, and won
reigns.previously: Magnus Erlingsson drowns at Fimreite. Sverre stands alone.
paragraphs: Sverre grew up in the Faroe Islands and trained as a priest. In about 1175, so he said, his mother told him a secret: his real father was King Sigurd Munn, one of Harald Gille's sons. Sverre sailed to Norway and joined the Birkebeiners, a ragged rebel band named after the birch bark they wrapped round their legs. He was soon their leader.

He turned out to be a brilliant guerrilla general and a gifted talker. He beat Erling Skakke at Kalvskinnet, near Trondheim, in 1179, and in 1184 caught Magnus Erlingsson's fleet at Fimreite. Magnus drowned and Sverre was king of all Norway. Keeping it was harder.

The bishops loathed him and backed a rival party, the Baglers, named after the bishop's crozier. The pope excommunicated Sverre and put Norway under an interdict. Sverre hit back with a fierce speech arguing that a king's power came straight from God. He was still fighting the Baglers when he died in Bergen in 1202.

claims.text: Sverre really was the son of King Sigurd Munn.
claims.note: We only have his word, passed on from his mother. His enemies called him an impostor, and historians are still split.

claims.text: Sverre helped write his own saga.
claims.note: The prologue of Sverris saga says Abbot Karl Jónsson wrote the first part with the king sitting over him, deciding what went in.

claims.text: On his deathbed he asked to lie with his face uncovered, so everyone could see whether excommunication had marked him.
claims.note: Sverris saga tells it. It reads like his last piece of propaganda.

reigns.hook: Sverre's son Haakon takes over and makes peace with the bishops. Norway can breathe again. But Sverre's widow is still at court, and she and her stepson do not get on.

reigns.previously: The bishops' party, the Baglers, rise against Sverre.
paragraphs: The Baglers, backed by the exiled bishops, chose Inge as their king against Sverre in 1196, claiming he was a son of the earlier king Magnus Erlingsson. They held eastern Norway around Oslo.
He fought Sverre for years without winning. In 1202 he was killed by his own followers.
reigns.hook: The Birkebeiners and Baglers keep fighting under new kings.

reigns.tagline: Sverre's son made peace, then dropped dead
reigns.previously: Sverre dies in Bergen, still at war with the bishops.
paragraphs: Haakon was Sverre's son from his rebel years and had fought beside him against the Baglers. On his deathbed in March 1202 Sverre said Haakon was his only living son and left him a letter with one piece of advice: make peace with the Church. When the news reached Nidaros the Birkebeiners took Haakon as their leader, and that spring he was hailed king.

He did what his father asked. The exiled bishops came home, Haakon gave them most of what they wanted, and Norway was freed from the pope's interdict. The Bagler party fell apart, and that autumn farmers in the Uplands killed its king, Inge Magnusson. For the first time in years Norway had one king and no war.

It lasted less than two years. Haakon clashed with his stepmother, Queen Margaret, a Swedish king's daughter, and his men took her young daughter from her when she tried to leave for home. At Christmas 1203 he fell ill after being bled and died on New Year's Day 1204, aged about 20. He had no wife and, as far as anyone knew, no children.

claims.text: Queen Margaret poisoned him.
claims.note: The Bagler sagas report the suspicion. A man who carried hot iron for her was badly burned, and she fled to Sweden. That is rumour and ordeal, not proof.

claims.text: Haakon ended the papal interdict by settling with the bishops.
claims.note: The bishops' return and the settlement of 1202 are well recorded.

claims.text: Haakon III was the father of Haakon IV, born after his death.
claims.note: Nobody knew of the boy until 1206. It rests on his mother Inga's word and her ordeal by hot iron in 1218. Most historians accept it, but it can't be proved.

reigns.hook: The new king is Sverre's grandson Guttorm, aged four. Real power goes to a hot-headed cousin, Haakon the Crazy. And a young woman from Varteig is carrying a secret.

reigns.tagline: Four years old, and king for seven months
reigns.previously: Haakon III dies on New Year's Day 1204. Poison is whispered.
paragraphs: Guttorm was the illegitimate son of Sverre's eldest son, Sigurd Lavard, who had died before his father. With Haakon III dead and no other heir in sight, the Birkebeiner leaders made the four-year-old king the very next day. Someone had to rule for him, so Sverre's nephew Haakon the Crazy was made an earl and given the army.

Haakon the Crazy was a fighter, and the Baglers took his rise as a sign there would be no peace. Their exiles in Denmark picked a new king, Erling Steinvegg, said to be a son of Magnus Erlingsson. In June 1204 King Valdemar II of Denmark sailed into the Oslofjord with a huge fleet to back him, and the Baglers soon held the whole region.

Guttorm was hailed king again at the Øyrating in Nidaros while his guardians got ready for war. Then, on 11 August 1204, the little boy fell ill and died. He was buried in Nidaros Cathedral. Haakon the Crazy wanted the crown for himself, but he had made too many enemies.

claims.text: Guttorm was poisoned by Christina, the Swedish noblewoman Haakon the Crazy married soon afterwards.
claims.note: Only the longer Bagler saga hints at it. Modern historians think it was Birkebeiner gossip after Haakon III's suspicious death.

claims.text: The child king girded Earl Haakon with a sword and sat him level with the throne.
claims.note: The Bagler sagas, written soon after, describe the ceremony. An earl normally sat lower than the king.

claims.text: Denmark backed the Baglers to win back its old hold over the Oslofjord.
claims.note: Valdemar II's 1204 expedition and the Baglers' oath to him are recorded in the Bagler sagas.

reigns.hook: Two kings dead in one year. The Birkebeiner warriors want Haakon the Crazy. The archbishop and the farmers of Trøndelag want his quiet younger half-brother, Inge. Somebody has to back down.

reigns.tagline: The quiet king who swam for his life
reigns.cameToPower: Chosen by the archbishop and farmers
reigns.previously: Little King Guttorm dies suddenly. The Birkebeiners need a king.
paragraphs: Inge Bårdsson was a king by compromise. His mother Cecilia was Sverre's half-sister and his father Bård a loyal Birkebeiner lord. The warriors wanted Inge's older half-brother, Haakon the Crazy, but the archbishop and the farmers of Trøndelag insisted on Inge. So Inge got the crown, and Haakon got the army and half the royal income.

The Baglers held the east and fought hard. On 22 April 1206 they burst into Nidaros during a wedding feast for Inge's sister. Inge escaped by swimming across the icy river Nid and was never fully well again. That same year the Birkebeiners learned of Haakon III's baby son, and the boy was brought to Inge's court.

In 1208 churchmen brokered peace at Kvitsøy. The Bagler king Philip gave up his title, kept the east as an earl and married Sverre's daughter Kristin, while Inge stayed sole king. Philip quietly went on calling himself king anyway. Haakon the Crazy died in 1214 and Inge took his lands. In April 1217 Inge fell ill in Nidaros, made his half-brother Skule an earl, and died.

claims.text: Inge swam the freezing river Nid to escape a surprise attack in 1206.
claims.note: The Bagler sagas, written during and just after his reign, tell the story in detail.

claims.text: Inge was a weak king.
claims.note: He never ruled all Norway and shared power with the Baglers. Others argue that keeping the peace took real strength.

claims.text: The oldest surviving Norwegian royal letter was issued by Inge's rival Philip, not by Inge.
claims.note: The letter dates from Inge's reign and shows Philip still acting as a king despite the 1208 deal.

reigns.hook: Inge leaves only an illegitimate son. The Birkebeiners have another candidate: the boy they rescued as a baby, Haakon III's son, now 13. Earl Skule has plans of his own.

reigns.tagline: The Bagler king who made peace
reigns.previously: The Baglers choose a new king to fight Inge II.
paragraphs: Philip was chosen king by the Bagler party in 1207, ruling eastern Norway. In 1208 he made peace with Inge II at Kvitsøy: he gave up the royal title and married Inge's niece, but in practice ruled his part as before.
He kept calling himself king anyway. He died in 1217, the same year as Inge, which let the two parties finally unite under Haakon IV.
reigns.hook: Both kings are dead, and the young Haakon IV inherits a united Norway.

reigns.tagline: The rescued baby who built an empire at sea
reigns.previously: Inge II dies in Nidaros. The Birkebeiners pick Sverre's grandson.
paragraphs: Haakon was born in 1204, months after his father, Sverre's son Haakon III, had died. The baby was in danger, so in the winter of 1206 Birkebeiner warriors carried him over the mountains to the safety of King Inge. When Inge died in 1217 the Birkebeiners made 13-year-old Haakon king. To prove who his father was, his mother Inga carried hot iron in Bergen in 1218, and her hands were judged unharmed.

Real power sat with Skule Bårdsson, Inge's half-brother, a proud earl who ran things while Haakon grew up. The two became rivals. Haakon married Skule's daughter Margaret, but in 1239 Skule declared himself king. He lost, and in 1240 he was killed after fleeing to a monastery. Norway's long civil wars were over at last.

Haakon was crowned by a papal legate in 1247 and made Norway a real European power. Greenland accepted his rule in 1261, and Iceland soon after. In 1263 he sailed to defend the Hebrides against Scotland. After an indecisive fight at Largs he fell ill in Orkney and died there in December.

claims.text: Birkebeiner skiers carried the baby Haakon across the mountains through a blizzard.
claims.note: Haakon's saga tells of a hard winter journey. The skis and the heroic details owe a lot to later retellings and Bergslien's famous painting.

claims.text: His mother Inga carried red-hot iron to prove his royal blood.
claims.note: Haakon's saga, written soon after his death, describes the ordeal in Bergen in 1218.

claims.text: On his deathbed he had sagas read aloud, finishing with his grandfather Sverre's.
claims.note: Sturla Thordarson's saga of Haakon, written for Haakon's son, records it.

reigns.hook: Haakon's son Magnus is already crowned. He inherits an empire at sea, a war with Scotland nobody can win, and a kingdom full of old local laws.

reigns.previously: Duke Skule tires of ruling for Haakon IV.
paragraphs: Skule had been regent for the young Haakon IV and was the most powerful man in Norway. In 1239 he had himself proclaimed king and attacked.

Haakon's forces beat him at Oslo. Skule took refuge in a monastery at Nidaros, which Haakon's men set on fire; he was killed as he came out in May 1240. It was the last battle of the Norwegian civil wars.
reigns.hook: The civil wars are over, and Haakon IV rules a Norway at its height.

reigns.tagline: The king who gave Norway one law for everyone
reigns.previously: Haakon the Old dies in Orkney after the clash at Largs.
paragraphs: Magnus was a younger son, but his brother Haakon the Young died in 1257, and Magnus was crowned alongside his father in 1261. Once Haakon was dead, Magnus decided the war in the west wasn't worth it. By the Treaty of Perth in 1266 he sold the Hebrides and the Isle of Man to Scotland for 4,000 marks, plus 100 marks a year. Orkney and Shetland stayed Norwegian.

His real passion was law. Each region of Norway had its own old law code. In 1274 Magnus replaced them with a single law for the whole country, the Landslov, then added a law for the towns. Iceland got a new law book too. The same rules now ran from Oslo to the Arctic.

He made a deal with the Church in 1277, the Concordat of Tønsberg, and gave his nobles European titles like baron and knight. He also hired the Icelander Sturla Thordarson to write his father's saga. Magnus died in Bergen in 1280, aged 42, leaving two young sons.

claims.text: He sold the Hebrides and Man to Scotland for 4,000 marks and 100 marks a year.
claims.note: The Treaty of Perth of 1266 survives and spells out the terms.

claims.text: His national law stayed the backbone of Norwegian law until 1687.
claims.note: Christian IV's Norwegian Law of 1604 was largely a translation of it. Christian V's Norwegian Code finally replaced it in 1687.

claims.text: A carved head in Stavanger Cathedral shows his real face.
claims.note: The head is dated to his lifetime or just after and is traditionally named as Magnus, but nothing on it proves who it is.

reigns.hook: Magnus's son Eric is only 12. The barons and the queen mother will run things, and they're about to pick a fight with the Church that will stick the boy with an ugly nickname.

reigns.tagline: The boy king whose daughter was meant to rule Scotland
reigns.cameToPower: Crowned as a boy in Bergen
reigns.previously: Magnus the Law-mender dies. His 12-year-old son takes the throne.
paragraphs: Eric was crowned in Bergen in 1280, aged 12, and for years his mother Ingeborg and a council of barons ruled for him. They quarrelled bitterly with the archbishop over Church rights and money, and churchmen never forgave it. In time the boy king took the blame, and the nickname Priest-hater.

In 1281 Eric married Margaret, daughter of King Alexander III of Scotland. She died in 1283 after giving birth to a girl, also called Margaret. Then Alexander's sons died, and in 1286 Alexander fell from his horse and was killed. The little Maid of Norway was now heir to Scotland. In 1290 she sailed to claim it, but died in Orkney on the way, aged seven.

At home Eric's government fought a trade war with the German Hanseatic towns, which blockaded Norway and won better terms in 1285. In 1293 Eric married again, to Isabel Bruce, sister of the future Robert the Bruce. They had a daughter, Ingebjørg. Eric died in 1299 with no son, so the crown passed to his brother Haakon.

claims.text: Eric hated priests.
claims.note: The nickname came from churchmen later on. The quarrel was really run by his regents while he was a boy.

claims.text: His daughter Margaret was recognised as heir to the Scottish throne.
claims.note: The Scottish lords swore to her in 1284, and the Treaty of Birgham in 1290 planned her marriage to Edward I's son.

claims.text: The Maid of Norway died of seasickness.
claims.note: Later stories blame a rough crossing. Nobody at the time recorded exactly what killed her.

reigns.hook: Eric's younger brother Haakon has spent years as duke of the lands around Oslo. Now he is king, and soon a woman will turn up in Bergen claiming to be Eric's dead daughter.

reigns.tagline: The castle builder who made Oslo matter
reigns.reignEnded: Died, leaving a grandson of three
reigns.previously: Eric II dies with no son. His brother Haakon takes the crown.
paragraphs: As a duke, Haakon had ruled eastern Norway from Oslo, and as king he kept his eyes there. Around 1300 he began Akershus Castle on a rock above Oslo harbour, and in the far north he built Vardøhus. Oslo grew into the heart of royal government, though Bergen stayed the biggest town.

Haakon wanted a strong crown and no over-mighty lords. In 1308 he ruled that the old noble titles of earl and lendmann should die out. He also had to deal with a ghost. In 1300 a woman arrived from Germany claiming to be the Maid of Norway, his dead niece. She was burned at Bergen in 1301.

He had no son. His daughter Ingebjørg married the Swedish duke Eric, and their son Magnus was born in 1316. When Haakon died in 1319, three-year-old Magnus was chosen king of Norway, and within weeks of Sweden as well. Haakon was the last king of Sverre's male line.

claims.text: The “False Margaret” who claimed to be the Maid of Norway was burned at Bergen in 1301.
claims.note: Icelandic annals record her execution, and a local cult honouring her grew up afterwards.

claims.text: Haakon made Oslo the capital of Norway.
claims.note: Many books say so, but medieval Norway had no fixed capital. Oslo's rise under him is clear; the label is later.

claims.text: Haakon's remains now lie in Akershus Castle.
claims.note: He was buried in St Mary's Church in Oslo. His remains were later moved to the royal mausoleum at Akershus.

reigns.hook: Norway's new king is a toddler who is also King of Sweden. One small boy, two crowns, and a kingdom about to be run from somewhere else.

reigns.tagline: A toddler with two crowns and a plague on the way
reigns.previously: Haakon V dies with no son. His crown passes to a little grandson.
paragraphs: Haakon V left no son, so the crown went to his daughter Ingebjørg's boy, Magnus. He was three. That same summer the Swedes picked him as their king too. For the first time Norway and Sweden shared a ruler, and Norway's royal line now ran through a Swedish family, the Folkungs. With a child on the throne, nobles and regents ran things for years.

Grown up, Magnus spent most of his time in Sweden, and Norwegians grumbled about an absent king. He bought the rich province of Scania from the Danes, which cost a fortune. In 1343 he agreed that his younger son Haakon would have Norway. Then, in 1349, a ship from England docked in Bergen carrying the Black Death. It tore through the country and left Norway far poorer and weaker for generations.

His later years were a slide. He lost Scania back to Denmark in 1360, was pushed off the Swedish throne in 1364 and spent years as a prisoner. He finished his days in Norway with his son and drowned in a shipwreck off the west coast in 1374.

claims.text: The Black Death reached Norway on a ship from England that docked in Bergen in 1349.
claims.note: Icelandic annals record the ship and the outbreak; historians accept the outline, if not every detail.

claims.text: The plague killed around half of all Norwegians.
claims.note: There are no counts. Estimates rest on later tax and farm records and range from about a third to well over half.

claims.text: His Swedish nickname, Smek, and his enemies' attacks mean he loved men.
claims.note: The charges come from hostile sources, including St Bridget's revelations, written when she had turned against him. Nothing proves it.

reigns.hook: Magnus can't hold two kingdoms together on his own. The deal is struck: Norway will go to his younger son Haakon. Haakon is barely out of nappies.

reigns.tagline: The king who married a ten-year-old girl and made history
reigns.previously: Magnus can't rule two kingdoms. Little Haakon is promised Norway.
paragraphs: Haakon was a small child when his father promised him Norway, so Magnus kept running things until the boy grew up and took charge in the 1350s. For a couple of years he was even king of Sweden as well, until the Swedish nobles threw out him and his father in 1364 and brought in a German, Albert of Mecklenburg. Haakon spent years trying to get Sweden back.

His big move was his wedding. In 1363 he married Margaret, the ten-year-old daughter of King Valdemar IV of Denmark. She was raised in Norway and learned the business of ruling from the start. Their only child, Olaf, was born in 1370. Haakon died in 1380, aged about 40, and was buried in Oslo. The boy king that followed had a mother who was going to be very hard to ignore.

claims.text: Margaret was only ten when she married Haakon.
claims.note: She was born in 1353 and the wedding took place in Copenhagen in 1363.

claims.text: Haakon's first bride, Elisabeth of Holstein, was blown off course on her way to him and kept in Denmark.
claims.note: Later chronicles tell the storm story. The broken engagement is certain; how it happened is less clear.

claims.text: Young Margaret wrote to Haakon complaining her household was going hungry.
claims.note: Her letter survives and is often quoted as a rare glimpse of royal money troubles.

reigns.hook: Haakon is dead. His son Olaf is ten and already king of Denmark. Now he has Norway too, and his mother Margaret is the one really holding the reins.

reigns.tagline: The boy who tied Norway to Denmark for 434 years
reigns.previously: Haakon VI dies. His young son is already king of Denmark.
paragraphs: Olaf's mother Margaret had already got him elected king of Denmark in 1376, when he was five. When his father died in 1380, Norway came to him as well. That made him the first king of both countries at once, and it started a union that lasted until 1814. A child couldn't rule, so Margaret did it for him, and she did it well.

Olaf also had a claim to Sweden through his father's family, and Margaret pushed it hard. Then, in August 1387, Olaf fell ill and died suddenly at Falsterbo castle in Scania. He was a teenager. The male line of Norway's old royal house ended with him, and people whispered about poison. All eyes turned to his mother.

claims.text: Olaf was poisoned.
claims.note: Rumours spread after his sudden death, but no contemporary source gives evidence. Illness is the likelier story.

claims.text: Years later a man turned up claiming to be Olaf, back from the dead.
claims.note: A 'False Olaf' appeared in Prussia around 1402. Margaret had him exposed and he was burned.

claims.text: His accession in 1380 began a union with Denmark that lasted until 1814.
claims.note: Norway shared its kings with Denmark from Olaf onwards, with only short breaks.

reigns.hook: Norway's king is dead and the old royal line is gone. Its nobles have no obvious heir. So they turn to the woman who has been running the country all along.

reigns.tagline: She ruled three kingdoms without ever being called queen
reigns.reignEnded: Died on her ship at Flensburg
reigns.previously: Olaf IV dies young. The old royal male line of Norway is gone.
paragraphs: Margaret had lost her son, but she kept her grip. Denmark named her its ruler within days, and in February 1388 the Norwegians chose her as their sovereign lady for life. Medieval law had no proper word for a woman in charge, so the Danes styled her 'lady and husband', master of the realm. In 1389 her armies beat the Swedish king Albert, and Sweden came over too.

She needed an heir, so she adopted her great-nephew Eric of Pomerania and had him crowned king of all three countries at Kalmar in 1397. That was the Kalmar Union. Eric was a figurehead while she lived. Margaret kept ruling until 1412, when she fell ill on her ship in Flensburg harbour and died. She was buried in Roskilde Cathedral.

claims.text: King Albert mocked her as 'King Breechless' and sent her a whetstone to sharpen her needles.
claims.note: The insults come from later Swedish chronicles. Nobody can show Albert actually said or sent them.

claims.text: The famous Kalmar Union document was never properly sealed into law.
claims.note: The surviving union letter is on paper with few seals. Historians still argue over whether it was a draft.

claims.text: She died of plague.
claims.note: Sources say she died suddenly on board ship; plague is the usual guess, not a proven fact.

reigns.hook: Margaret is dead. Her great-nephew Eric of Pomerania, crowned at Kalmar fifteen years ago, can finally rule three kingdoms himself, and he has a war in mind.

reigns.tagline: Crowned for three kingdoms, he ended up a Baltic raider
reigns.previously: Margaret dies. Eric of Pomerania rules all three kingdoms.
paragraphs: Eric was born Bogislaw, son of a Pomeranian duke, and Margaret picked him as her heir because his grandmother was her sister. She brought him north as a small boy, gave him a Nordic name and had him hailed King of Norway at the thing in Trondheim in 1389. In 1397 he was crowned for all three kingdoms at Kalmar. While Margaret lived, though, she did the ruling. Only when she died in 1412 did Eric get to use his crown.

He spent most of his reign fighting the counts of Holstein for Schleswig, and losing. To pay for it he brought in the Sound Toll in 1429, charging ships that passed Helsingør. Norway paid its share in other ways. Its castles and districts went to Danish and German bailiffs, and in 1436 the nobleman Amund Sigurdsson Bolt led a rising in the east that forced its way into Oslo.

In 1439 the Danish and Swedish councils deposed him. Eric had already sailed off to Visborg Castle on Gotland. Norway's council stayed loyal longest, but a king shut away on a Baltic island was no use to anyone, and in 1442 it gave up on him too. Eric lived on Gotland until 1449, then went home to Pomerania, where he died in 1459.

claims.text: From Gotland, the deposed king lived by raiding Baltic shipping.
claims.note: Hanseatic and Swedish complaints about ships seized by his men are well recorded. 'Pirate king' was his enemies' label, but the raids were real.

claims.text: When the Hanseatic fleet attacked Copenhagen in 1428, Queen Philippa ran the defence while Eric stayed away.
claims.note: Danish chronicles give her the credit. How far she commanded in person is hard to pin down.

claims.text: Eric beat Philippa after a failed attack on Stralsund, and she fled to a convent.
claims.note: She did die at Vadstena Abbey in 1430, but the beating story only turns up in later chronicles.

reigns.hook: Eric sits it out on Gotland. Denmark and Sweden have already crowned his nephew, a young German prince. Now Norway's lords head south to meet Christopher of Bavaria.

reigns.tagline: The German 'Bark King' who died at 31
reigns.cameToPower: Elected at Lödöse, crowned in Oslo
reigns.previously: Eric hides out on Gotland. Norway finally lets him go.
paragraphs: Christopher was a German prince, son of the Count Palatine of Neumarkt and of Eric's sister Catherine. The Danish council made him king in 1440 because he was young, foreign and, they hoped, easy to steer. Sweden took him in 1441. In June 1442 Norwegian lords met him at Lödöse, on the Göta river, and elected him king. On 2 July he was crowned in Oslo.

He never really governed Norway himself. Its council ran things at home, and the German merchants of the Hanseatic League kept their tight hold on Bergen's trade. Christopher made Copenhagen his base, married Dorothea of Brandenburg in 1445 and looked set for a long reign. Then in January 1448 he died suddenly at Helsingborg, aged 31. He had no children, and the union began to come apart.

claims.text: Swedes mocked him as the 'Bark King', blaming him for famine years when people mixed bark into their bread.
claims.note: The nickname is recorded in Swedish tradition. Blaming the king for bad harvests was a political jibe.

claims.text: It was said that if his council had asked him for the stars in the sky, he would have ordered them fetched.
claims.note: A later saying that sums up how pliant the councils thought he was. Nobody recorded him saying anything like it.

reigns.hook: Christopher dies with no heir. Sweden picks one of its own nobles, Karl Knutsson. Denmark picks a count from Oldenburg. Both want Norway, and Norway's council splits down the middle.

reigns.relationToPredecessor: Swedish noble, no kin of Christopher
reigns.reignEnded: Swedes made him give Norway up
reigns.previously: Christopher dies childless. Two new kings both want Norway.
paragraphs: Karl Knutsson was a rich Swedish noble who had risen in the revolt against Eric of Pomerania and later ran eastern Finland from Viborg Castle almost like a prince. When Christopher died, Karl's troops were on hand when the Swedes hailed their new king at the Stones of Mora in June 1448. He was the man they chose. He wanted the union back, with Sweden on top this time.

Norway's council split. In February 1449 one group declared for Karl, and in June another paid homage to Christian of Oldenburg, Denmark's new king. Karl moved fast. On 20 November 1449 he was crowned in Nidaros Cathedral in Trondheim. But Sweden's nobles had no wish to fight Denmark over Norway. In 1450 they made him sign his claim away. His Norwegian reign had lasted about seven months.
Karl stayed King of Sweden, on and off. He was driven out in 1457, came back, was driven out again, and was king for a third time when he died in Stockholm in 1470.

claims.text: Karl summed up his life in a rhyme: as lord of Fågelvik he was rich and mighty, as King of Sweden poor and unhappy.
claims.note: The verse is traditionally put in his mouth, but nobody can show he wrote it.

claims.text: His Swedish number, Charles VIII, is made up.
claims.note: It counts back from Charles IX, who took his number from a fictional list of early kings. In Norway he is Charles I.

reigns.hook: Karl gives up Norway. In summer 1450 Christian of Oldenburg sails north with a large fleet, heading for Trondheim and a crown of his own.

reigns.tagline: The broke king who pawned Orkney and Shetland
reigns.previously: Sweden makes Karl give Norway up. The way is clear for Denmark.
paragraphs: Christian was a young count of Oldenburg in north Germany. His uncle, the Duke of Schleswig, turned down the Danish crown in 1448 and put him forward instead, and the Danes elected him on condition that he marry Christopher's widow Dorothea. Once Sweden had made Karl Knutsson back off, Christian sailed to Norway with a large fleet. On 2 August 1450 he was crowned in Trondheim.

Weeks later, in Bergen, Danish and Norwegian councillors signed a treaty saying the two kingdoms would share one king for ever. It held until 1814. Christian also won Sweden in 1457, lost it in 1464 and was beaten at Brunkeberg outside Stockholm in 1471 trying to get it back. He founded the University of Copenhagen in 1479 and died in 1481.

He was always short of money. When his daughter Margaret married James III of Scotland, he couldn't pay the dowry. So in 1468 he pledged Norway's crown lands and rights in Orkney as security, and in 1469 Shetland too. The money never came, and the islands stayed with Scotland.

claims.text: The pledge was meant to be temporary.
claims.note: The deals allowed redemption, and later Danish-Norwegian kings raised it again and again. Scotland never agreed to sell them back.

claims.text: He was nicknamed 'the bottomless purse'.
claims.note: The jibe is repeated by later writers to sum up his debts. It is hard to trace to his own day.

reigns.hook: Christian dies in 1481. His son John expects all three crowns, but Norway's council has had enough of Danish bailiffs. It makes him wait.

reigns.tagline: The king Norway made wait two years
reigns.previously: Christian I dies. Norway's council refuses to rush.
paragraphs: John was Christian I's eldest surviving son and had been named heir years before. Denmark took him at once, but Norway's council held back. It was fed up with how his father had run the country, and in 1482 it even agreed with Sweden that neither would elect a king without the other. In January 1483, at Halmstad, the Danish and Norwegian councils settled terms. John was crowned in Trondheim on 20 July 1483.

He built Denmark's first permanent navy, won Sweden back in 1497 and lost it again in 1501. In 1500 his army was cut to pieces by peasant farmers in the marshes of Dithmarschen. Norway gave him trouble too. In 1501 the nobleman Knut Alvsson rose against his officials. In August 1502 Knut came to talks under a promise of safe conduct and was killed by the men of the king's commander, Henrik Krummedige.
John then sent his son Christian north as viceroy to keep Norway quiet. He died at Aalborg in February 1513 after a fall from his horse.

claims.text: Knut Alvsson was killed under a promise of safe conduct.
claims.note: Accounts agree he came aboard Krummedige's ship to talk terms. Whether the killing was planned is still argued over.

claims.text: John's flagship Gribshunden blew up and sank in 1495 while he was ashore.
claims.note: The wreck lies off Ronneby in Sweden and has been studied by archaeologists.

reigns.hook: John is dead. His son Christian already knows Norway well. He has spent years there crushing rebels, and fell for a Bergen girl named Dyveke.

reigns.tagline: He loved a Bergen girl and lost three crowns
reigns.previously: John dies after a riding accident. His son takes over.
paragraphs: Christian already knew Norway. His father made him viceroy there in 1506, and he crushed a rising in the east in 1508 and leaned hard on the Norwegian nobles. In Bergen he met Dyveke, a young woman of Dutch family, and she became his mistress. Her mother, Sigbrit Willoms, became his closest adviser. In 1514 he was crowned King of Norway in Oslo.

Dyveke died suddenly in 1517. Christian decided she had been poisoned and had the nobleman Torben Oxe executed after a trial by commoners, which horrified the aristocracy. In 1520 he conquered Sweden, then had more than eighty of its leading men put to death in the Stockholm Bloodbath. Sweden rose under Gustav Vasa and left the union for good.

His new laws favouring townsmen and peasants turned Denmark's nobles and bishops against him too. In January 1523 the Jutland nobles offered his crown to his uncle Frederick, and in April Christian sailed into exile in the Netherlands.

claims.text: Torben Oxe poisoned Dyveke with a bowl of cherries.
claims.note: The cherries story comes from later chronicles. Oxe was convicted on thin evidence, and she may simply have fallen ill.

claims.text: Swedes still call him Christian the Tyrant.
claims.note: The name comes from the Stockholm Bloodbath of November 1520 and is standard in Swedish.

reigns.hook: Christian is gone, but not finished. His uncle Frederick has taken Denmark, and Norway's council must decide whose side it is on.

reigns.tagline: The king who never once set foot in Norway
reigns.previously: Christian II flees to the Netherlands. Denmark crowns his uncle.
paragraphs: Frederick was Duke of Holstein and a younger son of Christian I, and Danish rebels offered him his nephew's throne in 1523. Norway's council took its time. With the new archbishop, Olav Engelbrektsson, among its leaders, it met in Bergen and drew up terms to protect Norway's laws, church and council. On 5 August 1524 it renounced Christian II, and on 23 August it elected Frederick. He never came to Norway, and ruled it from Gottorp and Copenhagen.

Frederick let Lutheran preachers work and protected some of them. Then in November 1531 Christian II came back with a fleet and landed in Norway. The archbishop and many others hailed him king again. Christian couldn't take Akershus Castle, and in 1532 he accepted a safe conduct to talk terms. Frederick refused to honour it and locked him up for life.
Frederick died at Gottorp in April 1533. The Danish council could not agree on his Lutheran son, so for the moment Norway had no king at all.

claims.text: Frederick broke a safe conduct to jail Christian II.
claims.note: His commanders in Norway gave the promise. Frederick and the Danish council chose not to keep it.

claims.text: Frederick may never have learned to speak Danish.
claims.note: He grew up a German-speaking duke in Holstein. Historians say it is not certain he ever mastered the language.

reigns.hook: Frederick is dead and Denmark can't agree on his son. Norway has no king, and Archbishop Olav Engelbrektsson sees one last chance to keep it Catholic.

reigns.title: The Archbishop's Last Stand
reigns.tagline: Four years without a king, and a churchman in charge
reigns.relationToPredecessor: After the death of Frederick I
reigns.cameToPower: Council ruled after Frederick I died
reigns.previously: Frederick I dies. Norway's council must find a king by itself.
paragraphs: When Frederick I died in April 1533, Norway's council of the realm expected a say in choosing the next king. Instead Denmark itself fell apart. Its council could not agree on an heir, and a civil war broke out, the Count's Feud. For four years Norway had no king it recognised, and the strongest man in the country was a churchman.

Olav Engelbrektsson, Archbishop of Nidaros, led the council and the Catholic party. He had backed the deposed Christian II in 1531–32, and he feared the next king would be a Lutheran. He was right. In 1534 Danish nobles chose Frederick's son Christian III, a firm Protestant. The archbishop had a stone fortress, Steinvikholm, on the fjord outside Trondheim, and he played for time.

At the start of 1536 his men killed his old rival, Vincens Lunge, in Trondheim. It was a fatal step. Christian III won the Count's Feud that summer, and in his charter that autumn he declared that Norway would never again be a kingdom of its own. Danish troops came north in spring 1537. On 1 April the archbishop sailed for the Netherlands with the church archives. He died in exile the next year.

claims.text: Christian III promised in 1536 that Norway would never again be a kingdom of its own.
claims.note: His charter said so in plain words. In practice Norway kept its own laws and some separate offices.

claims.text: Vincens Lunge was killed on the archbishop's orders.
claims.note: The archbishop's supporters did the killing. How far Olav planned it, or just let it happen, is still argued over.

claims.text: The archbishop looted Nidaros Cathedral as he fled.
claims.note: He took the archives and his own goods. He left St Olav's shrine behind, and modern historians think the charge was unfair.

reigns.hook: Norway's last Catholic archbishop is gone and its council abolished. Christian III is now master of Norway too, and he is bringing a new church with him.

reigns.tagline: On paper, he turned Norway into a Danish province
reigns.previously: Archbishop Olav flees Norway. Its council is abolished.
paragraphs: Christian was Frederick I's eldest son and a convinced Lutheran. Denmark's Catholic-led council balked at him, and a civil war, the Count's Feud, followed. Christian won it in 1536, arrested the Catholic bishops and made Denmark Lutheran. His charter that year said Norway would no longer be a kingdom of its own but part of Denmark, and its council of the realm was done away with.

In 1537, with the archbishop gone, Norway was his. The Lutheran Reformation came with him. Monasteries closed, church lands went to the crown, and in 1537 he named Gjeble Pederssøn as Norway's first Lutheran bishop. Danish-trained clergy took over, and Danish became the language of the church.

The promise to make Norway a mere province was never fully carried out. Norway kept its own laws and was still called a kingdom. Christian ruled in peace for another two decades and died on New Year's Day 1559.

claims.text: His 1536 charter turned Norway into a Danish province.
claims.note: The charter said so in plain words, but it was never put into practice. Norway kept its laws and its title of kingdom.

claims.text: The silver shrine of St Olav in Trondheim was carried off to Copenhagen and melted down.
claims.note: The shrine was taken in 1537. Church silver from across Norway went the same way to pay the king's war debts.

reigns.hook: Christian III dies on New Year's Day 1559. His son Frederick takes over a quiet kingdom, but across the border a hot-headed new Swedish king is spoiling for war.
