reigns.tagline: A long war with Sweden, then Tycho's island and Kronborg
reigns.previously: Christian III dies. Norway is now ruled entirely from Copenhagen.
paragraphs: Frederick loved hunting, feasting and a fight. In 1563 he went to war with Erik XIV of Sweden, and the Northern Seven Years' War dragged on until 1570. Norway was one of the battlefields. Swedish troops seized Trondheim in 1564, and in 1567 a Swedish army marched on Oslo, which went up in flames, and laid siege to Akershus Castle before being driven off.

Peace came at Stettin in 1570, with no land changing hands. Frederick spent the rest of his reign on splendour. He rebuilt Kronborg at Helsingør, the castle of Hamlet, and gave the astronomer Tycho Brahe the island of Hven to build his observatory. He died at Antvorskov in April 1588, leaving a ten-year-old heir.

claims.text: Frederick drank himself to death.
claims.note: His heavy drinking was well known and worried his own court. Whether it killed him is a guess.

claims.text: Kronborg is the 'Elsinore' of Shakespeare's Hamlet.
claims.note: Hamlet is set at Elsinore, the English name for Helsingør. English actors had played at the Danish court in the 1580s.

reigns.hook: Frederick dies in 1588. The new king, Christian IV, is ten years old. He will grow up to be the union king Norway remembers best.

reigns.tagline: The union king who kept coming to Norway and building towns
reigns.previously: Frederick II dies. His heir is a boy of ten.
paragraphs: Regents ran things until Christian was crowned in 1596. After that he ran everything himself, and unlike most union kings he kept turning up in Norway in person. In 1599 he sailed right round the North Cape to Vardø to show the flag in the far north. He took a close interest in Norway's mines, forts and towns.

Silver was found at Kongsberg in 1623, and he founded the mining town there the next year. When Oslo burned down in 1624, he had it rebuilt on a new site below Akershus Castle, with straight streets and stone houses, and named it Christiania after himself. The name stuck until 1925. In 1641 he founded Kristiansand on the south coast.

His wars went worse. He was beaten in the Thirty Years' War, and in 1643 Sweden attacked again. At Brömsebro in 1645 he had to give up Gotland, Ösel and two Norwegian provinces, Jämtland and Härjedalen. He died in 1648, after almost sixty years on the throne.

claims.text: He lost an eye in a sea battle and carried on directing the fight.
claims.note: Wounded by splinters at Kolberger Heide in July 1644, he lost his right eye. The scene became a national legend in Denmark.

claims.text: He picked the spot for Christiania himself, pointing with his stick: 'Here the town shall stand.'
claims.note: His decision to move the town is documented. The stick-pointing scene is a popular later story.

reigns.hook: Christian IV dies in 1648. His son Frederick III inherits debts, a battered army and a Swedish neighbour hungry for more.

reigns.tagline: He lost Trøndelag, won it back, then took all power
reigns.cameToPower: Elected after signing a strict charter
reigns.previously: Christian IV dies after sixty years. Sweden is circling.
paragraphs: Frederick was never meant to be king. He became heir only when his elder brother Christian died in 1647, and the Danish nobles made him sign a strict charter before they would elect him. In 1657 he declared war on Sweden to win back old losses, and it went horribly. In the winter of 1658 Charles X marched his army across the frozen straits to Zealand and dictated peace at Roskilde.

Norway paid heavily. At Roskilde it lost Trøndelag and Bohuslän, with the old border fortress of Båhus, while Denmark lost Skåne. Then Charles X attacked again. Copenhagen held out, and Norwegian troops won back Trondheim before the year was out. The peace of 1660 returned Trøndelag to Norway, but Bohuslän stayed Swedish.

Frederick turned the crisis into a power grab. In 1660 the crown became hereditary, and in 1661 he became absolute monarch, with Norway now a hereditary kingdom too. His King's Law of 1665 put almost no limits on the king. He died in Copenhagen in 1670.

claims.text: Charles X's army crossed the frozen sea to reach Copenhagen.
claims.note: The march across the ice of the Little and Great Belts in February 1658 is well documented, and a few men and horses fell through.

claims.text: The King's Law that made him absolute was kept out of print for decades.
claims.note: It was signed in 1665 but not published until 1709.

reigns.hook: Frederick III dies in 1670. His son Christian V inherits a crown with no strings attached, and a burning wish to win back what Sweden took.

reigns.tagline: The absolute king who gave Norway its law book
reigns.cameToPower: First heir under the 1665 King's Law
reigns.previously: Frederick III dies an absolute king. His son inherits it all.
paragraphs: Christian V was the first king to simply inherit total power. His father had torn up the old rules, so there was no council to bargain with and no charter to sign. Instead of a coronation he was anointed at Frederiksborg in 1671. He loved hunting, riding and parades, kept an official mistress, Sophie Amalie Moth, and left much of the paperwork to clever ministers.

The cleverest, Peder Griffenfeld, fell in 1676. He was led to the scaffold, reprieved at the last moment and kept a prisoner for 22 years, most of them on Munkholmen, the island fortress off Trondheim. Meanwhile Christian went to war to win back the lands lost to Sweden. Norwegians called it Gyldenløve's War, after the king's half-brother, their governor, whose troops pushed into Bohuslän. France forced a peace in 1679 and every gain was handed back.

His lasting gift was a book. In 1687 came Christian V's Norwegian Law, one code for the whole country, built on the Danish Law of 1683 but adjusted to Norwegian farms, fishing and inheritance. In 1698 he was hurt by a wounded stag during a hunt, and he died the next summer, aged 53.

claims.text: A handful of clauses from the 1687 Norwegian Law are still valid in Norway today.
claims.note: Norway's statute book still lists a few of its sections as in force. Nearly all the rest was replaced long ago.

claims.text: Griffenfeld was reprieved on the scaffold itself, at the very last moment.
claims.note: Several accounts of the day describe the last-second reprieve. The dramatic details vary between them.

claims.text: A wounded stag's attack killed the king.
claims.note: He was hurt in a hunt at Jægersborg in 1698, but years of heavy eating and drinking had worn him down. How far the injury caused his death is unclear.

reigns.hook: Christian V leaves a hard-working son, Frederick IV, and a dangerous neighbour. Sweden's teenage king, Charles XII, is about to turn the whole north upside down.

reigns.tagline: Charles XII invaded his Norway twice and died trying
reigns.previously: Christian V dies after a hunting accident. His son takes over.
paragraphs: Frederick IV was hard-working, sharp and never short of a love affair. He joined an alliance against Sweden in 1700 and was knocked out of the war within months. When he tried again in 1709, Sweden's soldier king Charles XII decided to strike back through Norway. In 1716 he marched in and took Christiania, but the garrison of Akershus Fortress held out.

Then a young naval officer from Trondheim, Peter Wessel, caught the Swedish supply fleet at Dynekilen and wrecked it. Charles had to pull back. Wessel was ennobled as Tordenskiold, 'thunder shield'. In 1718 Charles came again and besieged Fredriksten fortress at Halden. One night in late 1718 a bullet through the head killed him in the trenches. His second army, stuck in Trøndelag, retreated over the mountains in a blizzard and thousands froze.

At home Frederick married twice more without ending his first marriage, then made his last wife, Anna Sophie Reventlow, queen in 1721. That year the priest Hans Egede sailed from Bergen for Greenland with royal backing. To pay war debts, Norway's churches were auctioned off in the 1720s. Frederick died at Odense in 1730, the day after his 59th birthday.

claims.text: Charles XII was shot by one of his own men.
claims.note: His body was examined several times, last in 1917, without settling it. Many historians think a shot from the Norwegian side is the likeliest answer.

claims.text: Frederick secretly married Anna Sophie Reventlow while Queen Louise was still alive.
claims.note: The secret wedding was in 1712. He married her again openly and made her queen weeks after Louise died in 1721.

claims.text: Tordenskiold was killed in a duel at 30.
claims.note: He died near Hanover in 1720 after a quarrel over gambling, only four years after Dynekilen.

reigns.hook: Frederick dies worn out by wars and wives. His son Christian VI has hated the gambling and the mistresses for years. The fun at court is about to stop.

reigns.tagline: The pious king who sent every teenager to confirmation
reigns.previously: Frederick IV dies at Odense. His strict, pious son takes over.
paragraphs: Christian VI was everything his father wasn't: shy, sickly and devout. He was a Pietist, part of a movement that wanted faith felt in the heart and lived every day. At court the fun stopped and the Copenhagen theatre closed. His stepmother, Anna Sophie, was sent away to her manor at Clausholm.

In 1733 he and Queen Sophie Magdalene toured Norway, as far north as Trondheim. The big change he brought was in the parishes. From 1736 every young person had to be confirmed, which meant learning the catechism, and a school law of 1739 tried to put a teacher within reach of every farm. Southern Norway liked his grain monopoly much less. From 1735 it had to buy its corn from Denmark.

He kept out of every war, the first king of his line to manage that, and spent the money on palaces instead, including a grand new Christiansborg. He died at Hirschholm in August 1746, the day before his silver wedding anniversary.

claims.text: Christian VI was the first Oldenburg king never to go to war.
claims.note: Denmark-Norway stayed out of every conflict during his 16 years on the throne.

claims.text: Compulsory confirmation taught Norway to read.
claims.note: The law's aim was religious and reading was the means. Historians differ on how quickly literacy really spread on Norway's farms.

claims.text: The town of Kristiansund is named after him.
claims.note: It got its town charter in 1742 and took the reigning king's name.

reigns.hook: Christian VI is dead and the prayer meetings are over. His son Frederick V is young, charming and fond of a drink. The real work will be done by his ministers.

reigns.tagline: The king drank, his ministers ruled, the border got fixed
reigns.previously: Pious Christian VI dies. His easy-going son inherits.
paragraphs: Frederick V was handsome, friendly and far better liked than his father. He was also a heavy drinker who left government to able ministers, above all Adam Gottlob Moltke and the elder Bernstorff. They kept Denmark-Norway out of the Seven Years' War, and trade boomed. Norwegian timber, fish and shipping sold well.

For Norway the big event was a line on the map. In 1751 a treaty with Sweden fixed the long border through the mountains to the far north. An extra paper attached to it, the Lapp Codicil, let Sami herders keep crossing with their reindeer. In 1760 learned men in Trondheim founded a society for the sciences, the first of its kind in Norway.

Money ran short in the end. A head tax brought in in 1762 hit poor families hard, and in April 1765 about 2,000 farmers and fishermen poured into Bergen in protest, the so-called Stril War. Frederick died in January 1766, aged 42.

claims.text: The 1751 Lapp Codicil is still valid today.
claims.note: Norway and Sweden have never repealed it, though later reindeer-grazing agreements set the practical rules. It is often called the Sami Magna Carta.

claims.text: Frederick drank himself to death.
claims.note: He was a heavy drinker and in poor health by forty, but no record pins his death on drink alone.

claims.text: Leaders of the 1765 Bergen protest were sentenced to death, then spared.
claims.note: Their sentences were turned into life imprisonment. The extra tax was dropped in Norway in 1772.

reigns.hook: Frederick V dies young. His son, Christian VII, is not yet 17. Within months the court can tell something is badly wrong with the new king.

reigns.tagline: A mad king, a German doctor and a scandal in the palace
reigns.previously: Frederick V dies at 42. His teenage son inherits.
paragraphs: Christian VII was 16 when he became king, and he soon showed signs of serious mental illness. He married the British princess Caroline Matilda, and in 1768 a German doctor, Johann Friedrich Struensee, joined him on a long tour of Europe. Back home Struensee won the king's trust, then the queen's heart. By 1770 he was running the kingdom himself.

He fired off reforms, scrapping press censorship among other things. In January 1772 a palace coup brought him down. Struensee was executed, the queen was divorced and sent to Celle in Germany, and new men ruled in the king's name. In 1784 the 16-year-old Crown Prince Frederick took over in another palace coup, and he ran things from then on.

Norway's farmers had grievances of their own about officials, taxes and prices. In 1786 Christian Lofthus, a farmer from near Lillesand, took their complaints to Copenhagen. Back home thousands rallied to him, and in 1787 he was arrested. He died a prisoner at Akershus in 1797. The old king lived on as a figurehead until 1808.

claims.text: Christian VII had schizophrenia.
claims.note: It's a modern guess from descriptions of his behaviour. No diagnosis made centuries later can be certain.

claims.text: Struensee abolished censorship within months of taking charge.
claims.note: His decree of September 1770 gave Denmark-Norway one of Europe's freest presses, though limits soon came back.

claims.text: The king died of a stroke brought on by fright at the sight of Spanish troops.
claims.note: The story is often repeated but rests on thin evidence. He was old, ill and had long been confused.

reigns.hook: Old Christian VII is dead at last. His son Frederick, who has ruled for 24 years already, now wears the crown, and he's at war with Britain.

reigns.tagline: He backed Napoleon, and it cost him Norway
reigns.previously: Christian VII dies, after decades as a king in name only.
paragraphs: Frederick had ruled for his sick father since 1784. He freed Danish peasants from being tied to their estates and ended the grain monopoly that had squeezed southern Norway. Then the wars caught up with him. In 1807 Britain, afraid Napoleon would grab the Danish fleet, bombarded Copenhagen and sailed off with it. Frederick joined France.

That was a disaster for Norway. British warships blockaded the coast, grain from Denmark couldn't get through and people went hungry. Sweden attacked in 1808 and was beaten back by a Norwegian army under a Danish prince, Christian August. Sweden was so impressed it later chose him as its own crown prince.

Frederick did let Norway have its own university in Christiania, founded in 1811 and named after him. But Napoleon lost, and Frederick lost with him. On 14 January 1814 he signed the Treaty of Kiel, giving Norway to Sweden. Denmark kept Iceland, the Faroes and Greenland, old Norwegian lands. He reigned on in Denmark until 1839.

claims.text: Ibsen's poem Terje Vigen, about a man rowing grain past the British blockade, tells a true story.
claims.note: Ibsen wrote it in 1862. Grain runs in small boats did happen during the blockade, but Terje himself is fiction.

claims.text: The Danish state went bankrupt in 1813.
claims.note: Its finances collapsed under the war, and a new currency was brought in that January.

claims.text: Norway's first university was founded in 1811.
claims.note: The royal decree is dated 2 September 1811. It is today's University of Oslo.

reigns.hook: Norway has been signed away like a parcel. But the Danish prince governing in Christiania, Christian Frederick, has other ideas. He calls Norway's leading men together.

reigns.tagline: King for one summer, father of a constitution
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Cousin of Frederick VI of Denmark
reigns.previously: At Kiel, Frederick VI signs Norway over to Sweden.
paragraphs: Christian Frederick was the Danish heir-in-waiting and Denmark's governor in Norway. When the Treaty of Kiel gave Norway to Sweden, he refused to accept it. He called leading Norwegians together, and in spring 1814 an assembly met at Eidsvoll to write a constitution. On 17 May it was signed and he was elected king.

Sweden's crown prince, the former French marshal Bernadotte, wasn't having it. His troops attacked in late July and the short war went badly for Norway. In August the Convention of Moss ended the fighting. Sweden agreed to accept the new constitution, and Christian Frederick agreed to go. He abdicated in October and sailed home. In 1839 he became King Christian VIII of Denmark.

claims.text: Norway's constitution, signed on 17 May 1814, is still in force today.
claims.note: It has been amended many times but is one of the oldest written constitutions still in use.

claims.text: Christian Frederick's real aim was to win Norway back for Denmark.
claims.note: Swedes suspected it at the time. Historians still debate how far he was playing a long game for Copenhagen.

claims.text: The war with Sweden lasted only about two weeks.
claims.note: Fighting began at the end of July and stopped with the Convention of Moss on 14 August 1814.

reigns.hook: Christian Frederick sails away. Norway keeps its constitution and parliament, but the king will be Swedish. The Storting elects Sweden's old Charles XIII, who becomes Norway's Charles II.

reigns.tagline: Norway's first Swedish king: old, ill and childless
reigns.previously: Christian Frederick abdicates. Norway keeps its constitution.
paragraphs: Charles had become King of Sweden in 1809, after a coup threw out his nephew, Gustav IV Adolf. He was 60, worn out and childless, and a heart attack that year left him barely able to work. So the Swedes went looking for an heir. Their first pick, Norway's own commander Christian August, died suddenly in 1810. Their second was a French marshal, Jean-Baptiste Bernadotte.

Bernadotte, now Crown Prince Charles John, was the man who forced Norway into line in 1814. After the Moss convention the Storting rewrote the constitution to fit a shared king, and on 4 November 1814 it elected Charles as King of Norway. The Act of Union of 1815 set the deal down: one king, two kingdoms, each with its own laws, army and parliament.
Charles was king in name and Bernadotte did the ruling. A keen Freemason with a taste for mystics, the old king spent his last years in poor health and died in Stockholm in February 1818.

claims.text: Charles founded an order of knighthood just for Freemasons.
claims.note: The Order of Charles XIII, set up in 1811, is still given only to senior Swedish Freemasons.

claims.text: The union with Sweden was a partnership of equals.
claims.note: On paper, yes. In practice Sweden ran foreign policy, and Norwegians spent 90 years complaining about it.

reigns.hook: The old king is dead. Now the man who really ran things, Napoleon's former marshal, takes the throne himself, and he'll be crowned in Trondheim.

reigns.tagline: From French private to king in Nidaros Cathedral
reigns.previously: Old Charles II dies. Bernadotte is king at last.
paragraphs: Jean-Baptiste Bernadotte joined the French army as a private at 17 and rose to be one of Napoleon's marshals. Sweden picked him as crown prince in 1810, and he turned on his old boss, fighting against Napoleon in 1813. His reward was Norway. As King Charles John he was crowned in Nidaros Cathedral in Trondheim on 7 September 1818.

He never properly learned Swedish or Norwegian, and he never liked Norway's constitution. He pressed the Storting for an absolute veto and more powers, and it kept saying no. In 1821 it abolished Norway's nobility over his objections. He frowned on 17 May parties too, and in 1829 troops and police broke up a crowd in Christiania's market square, the 'Battle of the Square'.

Even so, he grew popular with time. He began the Royal Palace in Christiania, and the main street leading up to it still carries his name, Karl Johans gate. He died in Stockholm in 1844, aged 81, founder of a dynasty that still sits on Sweden's throne.

claims.text: He had 'Death to kings' tattooed on his arm.
claims.note: The tale turns up in an 1833 French play and later gossip. There's no reliable record of anyone seeing such a tattoo.

claims.text: The Storting abolished the nobility in 1821 against the king's veto.
claims.note: A bill passed unchanged by three separately elected Stortings became law without the king. This one did.

reigns.hook: Bernadotte dies after 26 years on the throne. His only son, Oscar, Napoleon's godson, takes over, and he's in a far friendlier mood towards Norway.

reigns.tagline: Napoleon's godson, and a much kinder king to Norway
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Only son of Charles III John
reigns.previously: Bernadotte dies, still at odds with the Storting.
paragraphs: Oscar was born in Paris, with Napoleon as his godfather, and came to Sweden as a boy of 11. Unlike his father he spoke the language and had a taste for reform. He had served twice as viceroy in Norway, in 1824 and 1833, and he set out to make Norwegians feel like equal partners.

In 1844 he gave Norway and Sweden flags of equal standing, each with a shared union mark in the corner. Norwegians nicknamed the mark 'the herring salad'. In 1847 he founded the Order of St Olav. When Denmark fought Prussia in 1848, he sent Swedish and Norwegian troops to Funen to stand by it.

At home in Norway, Marcus Thrane's movement of workers and cottars grew fast around 1850, and its leaders were jailed. From 1857 Oscar was too ill to rule, and his son Charles acted as regent. He died in Stockholm in July 1859, four days after his 60th birthday.

claims.text: Napoleon was his godfather and chose his name.
claims.note: Napoleon picked Oscar from the Ossian poems he loved.

claims.text: Norwegians called the union mark 'the herring salad'.
claims.note: The nickname, sildesalaten, mocked its jumble of colours. The mark was taken out of Norway's merchant flag in 1899.

reigns.hook: Oscar I dies after two years as an invalid. His son Charles, tall, loud and popular, already knows the job, and he has made Norway a promise.

reigns.tagline: The jolly painter king who couldn't keep his promises
reigns.previously: Oscar I dies after years of illness. His son Charles takes over.
paragraphs: Charles was big, cheerful and easy to like. He painted landscapes, wrote verse and loved a party, and people called him 'Crown-Charlie'. He knew Norway, having been viceroy there in 1856 and 1857. Norwegians hated the post of stattholder, a governor who stood in for the king in Christiania, and Charles let them think he would scrap it.

In December 1859 the Storting voted to do just that. The Swedes were furious that Norway had acted alone, and Charles backed down and refused to sign. Norway felt snubbed, but he was still crowned in Nidaros Cathedral in 1860. The post was finally abolished in 1873.

He dreamed of a united Scandinavia and told his friend Frederick VII of Denmark he would help against the Germans. When war came in 1864, his ministers said no and no troops went. Charles died in Malmö in 1872, aged 46. His only son had died as a baby, so his brother Oscar inherited. Weeks earlier his daughter Louise had given birth to a Danish prince called Carl.

claims.text: Charles promised Denmark military help in 1864 and didn't deliver.
claims.note: He made warm promises to Frederick VII in 1863, but how binding they were is argued over. His cabinets in both countries refused to back them.

claims.text: His grandson became King Haakon VII of Norway.
claims.note: Prince Carl of Denmark, born in August 1872 to Charles's daughter Louise, was elected Norway's king in 1905.

reigns.hook: Charles dies without a son. His brother Oscar, a poet and naval officer, inherits two crowns and a Storting that wants real power.

reigns.tagline: The last union king, voted out of a job by the Storting
reigns.reignEnded: Storting said he'd ceased to be king
reigns.previously: Charles IV dies without a son. His brother Oscar inherits.
paragraphs: Oscar II was clever, vain and well read, a naval officer who wrote poetry and history. He was crowned in Trondheim in 1873 and started well by letting the hated stattholder post go. Then he ran into Norway's new politics. The Storting wanted the king's ministers to answer to it, and Oscar used his veto again and again.

In 1884 the Storting's majority impeached the whole cabinet and won. Oscar had to make the opposition leader, Johan Sverdrup, prime minister, and from then on governments needed the Storting's backing. The next fight was over consuls. Norway had one of the world's biggest merchant fleets and wanted its own consuls abroad. Sweden said foreign affairs were a joint matter.

In May 1905 Oscar refused to sign Norway's consul law, and the government resigned. He said he could not form a new one. On 7 June the Storting declared that he had ceased to function as king and the union was over. After a referendum and talks at Karlstad, Oscar renounced Norway's crown on 26 October 1905. He died in Stockholm two years later.

claims.text: The Storting offered to take one of Oscar's own relatives as Norway's new king.
claims.note: Its address of 7 June 1905 asked for a Bernadotte prince. Oscar turned the offer down.

claims.text: The 1884 crisis brought parliamentary government to Norway.
claims.note: Historians date the breakthrough to 1884, though the rule was only written into the constitution in 2007.

claims.text: Sweden and Norway came close to war in 1905.
claims.note: Both sides moved troops to the border, but how near they came to fighting is still argued over.

reigns.hook: Norway is a kingdom without a king. The Storting's favourite is a young Danish prince, Carl, grandson of Charles IV. He'll only come if the people vote for him.

reigns.tagline: The elected king who told Hitler no
reigns.previously: The Storting declares Oscar II no longer king. The union is over.
paragraphs: Prince Carl of Denmark was a navy officer married to Maud, daughter of Britain's Edward VII. Asked to be Norway's king, he insisted the people vote first. In November 1905 a big majority said yes. The Storting elected him, he took the old royal name Haakon, and his toddler son Alexander became Olav. He set out to be a king for everyone.

Then came 9 April 1940. Germany invaded, and Hitler demanded that Haakon appoint the Nazi collaborator Vidkun Quisling as prime minister. Haakon told his government he would abdicate before he did that. The government backed him. German bombers hunted the royal party across the country, and in June the king sailed for Britain.
From London his radio speeches kept Norway going. His monogram, H7, was painted on walls across the occupied country. He came home in triumph on 7 June 1945 and reigned until his death in 1957.

claims.text: Haakon said he would abdicate rather than appoint Quisling.
claims.note: Ministers who were at the Nybergsund meeting on 10 April 1940 recorded his words.

claims.text: About 79 per cent of voters said yes to him as king in 1905.
claims.note: Official referendum results: roughly 259,500 for and 69,300 against.

reigns.tagline: The people's king who took the tram to go skiing
reigns.previously: Haakon VII, Norway's war hero king, dies in 1957.
paragraphs: Olav was born in England and arrived in Norway as a toddler. He grew up sporty. He jumped at Holmenkollen and won Olympic gold in sailing in 1928. In the war he went into exile with his father and in 1944 was made chief of Norway's armed forces. His wife, Crown Princess Märtha, died in 1954, so he became king a widower.

He was easy to like: warm, funny, and not stuffy at all. During the 1973 oil crisis, Sunday driving was banned. So the king put his skis on his shoulder and took the tram up to the hills like everyone else, and the photo went round the world. When he died in January 1991, Oslo people placed thousands of candles in the snow outside the palace.

claims.text: Olav insisted on paying for his tram ticket during the 1973 driving ban.
claims.note: Press reports and photos at the time covered the trip. The ticket detail has been retold ever since.

claims.text: Asked about bodyguards, he said he had four million of them.
claims.note: The line is always credited to him, but there is no reliable record of when or where he said it.

claims.text: He won Olympic gold in sailing at Amsterdam in 1928.
claims.note: He crewed the winning Norwegian boat in the six-metre class.

reigns.tagline: The king who waited nine years to marry a commoner
reigns.previously: Olav V, the people's king, dies in January 1991.
paragraphs: Harald was born in 1937, the first prince born in Norway in 567 years. He spent the war in the United States with his mother. As a young man he fell for Sonja Haraldsen, a shopkeeper's daughter. A commoner as queen was a big deal, and the couple waited nine years before King Olav agreed. They married in 1968.

Like his father he loved sailing, and he carried Norway's flag at the Olympics. As king he chose a blessing in Nidaros Cathedral in 1991 instead of a coronation. After the terror attacks of July 2011 he and Sonja led the nation's mourning. In a 2016 speech he said Norwegians are many things: young and old, from north and south, believers and not, and of every origin.

claims.text: Harald and Sonja waited nine years before they were allowed to marry.
claims.note: Documented by the royal court; the engagement was announced in March 1968.

claims.text: He was the first prince born in Norway since the Middle Ages.
claims.note: The royal court notes he was the first born on Norwegian soil since Olav IV in 1370.

claims.text: Instead of a crown, he chose a blessing at Nidaros Cathedral in 1991.
claims.note: Coronations were removed from the constitution in 1908. Harald and Sonja were blessed in Trondheim in June 1991.

reigns.tagline: The crown prince who waited, and is now king
reigns.previously: Harald V dies in August 2026 after 35 years on the throne.
paragraphs: Haakon was born in 1973 and grew up as heir to a low-key, modern monarchy. He trained at the naval academy, studied political science at the University of California, Berkeley, and took a master's at the London School of Economics. In 2001 he married Mette-Marit Tjessem Høiby, a single mother whose past had filled the newspapers. Days before the wedding she faced the press and asked people to judge her on who she was now.

Their daughter, Princess Ingrid Alexandra, was born in 2004. Under the 1990 change to the constitution, which let the eldest child inherit whatever their sex, she is next in line. Haakon stood in as regent several times when his father was ill. When Harald V died on 28 August 2026, Haakon became king that day, taking the name Haakon VIII, and swore his oath before the Storting days later.

claims.text: Mette-Marit spoke openly about her past at a press conference before the wedding.
claims.note: Her August 2001 press conference was broadcast and widely reported in Norway and abroad.

claims.text: Princess Ingrid Alexandra is set to be the first woman to inherit the Norwegian throne under equal succession.
claims.note: The 1990 constitutional change applies to those born after it; she is the first heir it affects.
